lessons.title: How markets work
body: Every price you see is the last point where a buyer and a seller agreed. When more people want to buy than sell at the current price, price rises until enough sellers appear. Trading is the business of judging which side is about to win, and by how much.
## The main asset classes
- Forex: currencies traded in pairs. EUR/USD at 1.12 means one euro costs 1.12 US dollars. Open 24 hours a day, five days a week.
- Commodities: gold, silver, oil, gas, metals and crops. Priced mostly in US dollars, so a weaker dollar tends to lift them.
- Indices: a basket of stocks, like the S&P 500 or Nifty 50. They show the health of a whole market in one number.
- Stocks: shares in one company. Driven by earnings, guidance and the wider market mood.
- Crypto: digital assets like Bitcoin. Trade every day of the year and move faster than most markets.
## How you trade them

You can own the asset itself (buying shares or physical gold), or trade a contract that follows its price, such as futures or CFDs. Contracts let you sell first (go short) and use leverage, which magnifies both gains and losses.
## Bid, ask and spread

The bid is what buyers pay, the ask is what sellers want, and the gap is the spread. You buy at the ask and sell at the bid, so every trade starts slightly negative. Tight spreads on liquid markets like EUR/USD keep that cost small.

lessons.title: Reading a price chart
body: A candlestick shows four prices for one period: open, high, low and close. A green (rising) candle closed above its open; a red (falling) candle closed below. The thin wicks show how far price stretched before pulling back.
## Timeframes

The same market looks different on a 5-minute chart and a daily chart. Professionals start on a higher timeframe to find the trend and key levels, then drop to a lower one to time entries. A rule of thumb: trade in the direction of the timeframe above yours.
## What candles tell you
- Long upper wick: buyers pushed up but sellers took control. Often seen at resistance.
- Long lower wick: sellers pushed down but buyers stepped in. Often seen at support.
- Large body with small wicks: one side dominated the whole period.
- Small body, wicks on both sides: indecision.
## Volume
Volume shows how much traded. A breakout on rising volume is more convincing than one on thin volume. Forex has no central volume figure, so traders use tick volume or futures volume instead.

lessons.title: Support, resistance and key levels
body: Support is a price area where buying has repeatedly stopped a fall. Resistance is where selling has repeatedly stopped a rise. They work because many traders watch the same levels and place orders around them.
## Where key levels come from
- Previous highs and lows, especially daily and weekly ones.
- Round numbers like $4,000 gold, 1.1000 EUR/USD or 25,000 Nifty.
- Pivot points, calculated from the previous day's high, low and close. The desk lists P, R1–R3 and S1–S3 for many markets.
- Moving averages such as the 50-day and 200-day.
- Gaps: price areas skipped between one close and the next open, which often get revisited.
## Breakouts and role reversal

When price breaks through resistance and holds, that old resistance often becomes new support. Waiting for a close beyond the level, rather than a brief poke through it, filters out many false breakouts.
## How Tina's FX uses them
Each desk call names a trigger level for a long and a short scenario. WAIT means price is between them. The call only flips to BUY or SELL once price closes beyond a trigger.

lessons.title: Trends and moving averages
body: An uptrend makes higher highs and higher lows; a downtrend makes lower highs and lower lows. Most strategies either follow the trend or trade a range when there is no trend.
## Moving averages

A moving average smooths price by averaging the last N closes. The 20-period shows the short-term direction, the 50 the medium term and the 200 the long term. An exponential moving average (EMA) weighs recent prices more and reacts faster.
- Price above a rising 200-day average: the long-term trend is up.
- 50-day crossing above the 200-day: often called a golden cross, a bullish signal.
- 50-day crossing below the 200-day: a death cross, a bearish signal.
## Using them well

Moving averages lag, so they confirm trends rather than predict them. In sideways markets they cross back and forth and give false signals. Combine them with levels and momentum instead of trading crosses alone.

lessons.title: Momentum: RSI, MACD and Bollinger Bands
body: ## RSI (Relative Strength Index)

RSI measures the speed of recent moves on a 0–100 scale, usually over 14 periods. Above 70 is called overbought and below 30 oversold. In strong trends RSI can stay overbought or oversold for a long time, so treat extremes as a warning, not a signal on their own. A divergence, where price makes a new high but RSI does not, can hint that momentum is fading.
## MACD

MACD is the gap between the 12- and 26-period EMAs, with a 9-period signal line. The histogram shows the gap between the two. A rising histogram means momentum is building; a MACD cross above the signal line is a common bullish trigger.
## Bollinger Bands

Bands set two standard deviations above and below a 20-period average. They widen when volatility rises and narrow when it falls. A tight squeeze often comes before a big move. Touching a band is not a signal by itself; in trends price can ride along a band.
## Live technical rating

Every market page on this site shows TradingView's live technical rating, which summarises many moving averages and oscillators into Strong sell to Strong buy. It's a quick read on momentum, not a trade plan.

lessons.title: Risk management: the 1% rule and position sizing
body: “In trading, you need to learn how to manage your trades when you are in losses, not the profit.” — Tina Singh, 1970–2026
The fastest way to fail as a trader is not a bad call. It is one trade that is too big. Risk management decides how long you survive, and survival is what gives skill time to show.
## The 1% rule
Risk no more than 1% (some use 2%) of your account on any single trade. With a $10,000 account that is $100. Ten losses in a row would then cost about 10%, which is recoverable.
## Position sizing

Decide the stop first, then the size. Size = money you are willing to lose ÷ distance to your stop. If you risk $100 and your stop on gold is $10 away, you can trade 10 ounces. The position-size calculator in Tools does this for you.
## Why losses hurt more than gains help
- Lose 10% and you need +11% to get back.
- Lose 25% and you need +33%.
- Lose 50% and you need +100%.
## Leverage

Leverage lets a small deposit control a large position. It does not change how much you can lose per point; it only makes it easier to take positions too big for your account. Size by risk, never by how much leverage is available.

lessons.title: Risk to reward and win rate
body: Risk to reward (R:R) compares what you can lose to what you aim to win. A trade risking $100 to make $200 is 1:2.
## Breakeven win rate
The better your R:R, the fewer trades you need to win. At 1:1 you must win more than 50% of trades to profit. At 1:2 you need just over 33%. At 1:3, 25%. The formula is 1 ÷ (1 + R).
## Expectancy

Expectancy = (win rate × average win) − (loss rate × average loss). A positive number over many trades is the only real proof that a method works. That is why the desk keeps a public record of every call.
## Practical rules
- Never move a stop further away to avoid a loss.
- Take partial profit at the first target and move the stop to breakeven if the plan allows.
- Skip trades where the nearest obstacle sits closer than your target.

lessons.title: Trading psychology
body: Most trading mistakes are emotional: chasing a move after missing it, holding a loser because closing it feels like admitting you were wrong, or doubling size to win back a loss.
## Mushkil waqt, commando sakht
Tina’s motto. Hard markets reward the trader with rules. Write the plan before the trade: entry, stop, targets and size. Then your job during the trade is to follow the plan, not to invent a new one.
## Habits that help
- Keep a journal: why you entered, what you felt, what happened.
- Set a daily loss limit and stop trading for the day when you hit it.
- Trade smaller after a losing streak, not bigger.
- Don't trade into major news like CPI or a central-bank decision unless that is your strategy.
- Judge yourself on following the process, not on single outcomes.

lessons.title: What moves markets: rates, inflation, the dollar and oil
body: Behind every chart are a few big forces. Knowing them explains why many markets move together.
## Interest rates and central banks

Central banks like the US Federal Reserve set short-term interest rates. Higher rates make a currency more attractive and weigh on stocks, gold and crypto, because cash and bonds pay more. Markets move most when a decision differs from what was expected, which is why traders watch rate odds such as CME FedWatch.
## Inflation

Inflation data, especially the US CPI, shapes rate expectations. A hotter print than expected raises the odds of hikes, often lifting the dollar and yields and hitting gold and tech stocks, as happened on 14 October 2026.
## The US dollar

Most commodities are priced in dollars. A stronger dollar makes them more expensive for everyone else and tends to push prices down. The Dollar Index (DXY) measures the dollar against six major currencies.
## Bond yields
The US 10-year yield is the world's benchmark borrowing cost. Rising yields compete with non-yielding assets like gold and pressure high-growth stocks.
## Oil and geopolitics
Oil feeds into inflation and moves on supply risks, such as conflict in the Middle East or OPEC+ decisions. Gulf economies and markets are closely tied to its price.
## The calendar
High-impact releases: US CPI, jobs (non-farm payrolls), PCE inflation, central-bank decisions and big tech earnings. The Calendar page lists them live.

lessons.title: Forex primer
body: Forex is the largest market in the world. Currencies trade in pairs: buying EUR/USD means buying euros and selling dollars.
## Pips and lots
- A pip is the fourth decimal for most pairs (0.0001) and the second for yen pairs (0.01).
- A standard lot is 100,000 units of the base currency; a mini lot 10,000; a micro lot 1,000.
- On a standard lot of a USD-quoted pair like EUR/USD, one pip is worth $10.
## Sessions

Liquidity moves around the world: Sydney and Tokyo, then London, then New York. The London–New York overlap, roughly 4 pm to 8 pm Dubai time, is usually the most active window. The Tools page shows which sessions are open right now.
## What drives currencies

Interest-rate differences, inflation, growth, trade flows and risk mood. The yen and Swiss franc often rise in risk-off periods; the Australian dollar tends to follow global growth and commodity prices.

lessons.title: Gold and silver primer
body: Gold is money that no government prints. It tends to do well when real interest rates fall, when the dollar weakens, and in times of stress. Central banks have been major buyers in recent years.
## Key facts
- Quoted as XAU/USD, dollars per troy ounce (31.1 grams).
- A standard contract is 100 ounces, so a $1 move equals $100 per lot.
- Most active during the London and New York sessions.
## What moves gold
- Real yields and Fed expectations.
- The dollar index.
- Geopolitical risk and safe-haven demand.
- Central-bank and ETF buying or selling.
## Silver
Silver follows gold but swings harder, because it is also an industrial metal used in solar panels and electronics. The gold-to-silver ratio shows how many ounces of silver one ounce of gold buys.

lessons.title: Stock indices primer
body: An index tracks a basket of stocks. Trading an index gives exposure to a whole market without picking single companies.
## The big ones
- S&P 500: 500 large US companies, the global benchmark.
- Nasdaq: tech-heavy; very sensitive to rates and AI sentiment.
- Dow Jones: 30 large US companies, price-weighted.
- DAX, FTSE, CAC: Germany, UK and France.
- Nikkei, Hang Seng, Shanghai: Japan, Hong Kong and mainland China.
## What moves them
Earnings, interest rates, economic growth and risk appetite. A handful of megacaps now drive much of the US indices, so their earnings dates matter for everyone.
## The VIX
The VIX measures expected S&P 500 volatility over the next 30 days. It usually rises when stocks fall sharply, which is why it is called the fear gauge.

lessons.title: India primer: Nifty, Sensex and Bank Nifty
body: India is one of the world's largest and fastest-growing stock markets, with two exchanges: the NSE and the BSE.
## The indices
- Nifty 50: the 50 largest NSE companies, India's main benchmark.
- Sensex: 30 large BSE companies, India's oldest index.
- Nifty Bank: the major banks, the most actively traded index for derivatives.
## Hours and rules
Regular trading runs 9:15 am to 3:30 pm India time, Monday to Friday, which is 7:45 am to 2:00 pm in Dubai. India is regulated by SEBI.
## What moves Indian markets
Foreign investor flows, the rupee, oil prices (India imports most of its oil), RBI rate decisions, quarterly earnings and government policy.

lessons.title: Gulf markets primer: Dubai, Abu Dhabi and Saudi
body: Gulf stock markets have grown fast with listings of banks, property developers, utilities and energy giants.
## The exchanges
- Dubai Financial Market (DFM): Emaar, Emirates NBD, Dubai Islamic Bank, Salik and more. Benchmark: DFM General Index.
- Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange (ADX): First Abu Dhabi Bank, ADNOC companies, Aldar. Benchmark: FTSE ADX General.
- Saudi Exchange (Tadawul): Saudi Aramco, Al Rajhi Bank, SABIC. Benchmark: TASI.
## Hours
UAE exchanges trade Monday to Friday, generally 10:00 am to 3:00 pm Dubai time. Tadawul trades Sunday to Thursday.
## What moves Gulf markets
Oil prices, US interest rates (the dirham and riyal are pegged to the dollar, so local rates follow the Fed), property cycles, IPOs and regional geopolitics.

lessons.title: Crypto primer
body: Crypto trades every hour of every day. Moves of 5–10% in a day are common, so position sizes must be smaller than in forex or indices.
## The majors
- Bitcoin: the largest by value, with a fixed supply of 21 million coins.
- Ethereum: a platform for smart contracts and tokens.
- Solana, XRP, BNB and others: faster-moving and riskier.
## What moves crypto
Liquidity and interest rates, spot ETF flows, regulation, big exchange events, and overall risk appetite. Bitcoin often trades like a high-beta tech stock in stress.
## Risks to respect
Weekend gaps in other markets don't apply, but weekend liquidity is thin. Use regulated exchanges, protect your accounts, and never keep more on an exchange than you are trading.

glossary: Ask
The price at which sellers offer to sell. You buy at the ask.
ATR
Average True Range: the average size of a period's price range, used to set stops relative to volatility.
Basis point
One hundredth of a percentage point. A 25 basis point hike is 0.25%.
Bear market
A sustained fall, often defined as 20% or more from a high.
Bid
The price at which buyers will buy. You sell at the bid.
Bollinger Bands
Bands two standard deviations around a moving average that widen and narrow with volatility.
Breakout
A move beyond a support or resistance level, ideally confirmed by a close.
Bull market
A sustained rise, often defined as 20% or more from a low.
Candlestick
A chart bar showing the open, high, low and close for one period.
CFD
Contract for difference: a contract that pays the change in an asset's price without owning it.
CPI
Consumer Price Index, the main measure of inflation.
Death cross
When the 50-day moving average crosses below the 200-day.
Divergence
When price and an indicator like RSI move in opposite directions, hinting at fading momentum.
Drawdown
The fall from an account's peak to its lowest point.
DXY
The US Dollar Index, measuring the dollar against six major currencies.
EMA
Exponential moving average, weighted towards recent prices.
Expectancy
The average amount a strategy wins or loses per trade over many trades.
FOMC
Federal Open Market Committee, the Fed group that sets US interest rates.
Futures
A contract to buy or sell an asset at a set price on a future date.
Gap
A jump in price between one close and the next open, leaving no trades in between.
Golden cross
When the 50-day moving average crosses above the 200-day.
Hawkish
Leaning towards higher interest rates to fight inflation.
Dovish
Leaning towards lower interest rates to support growth.
Hedge
A position taken to offset the risk of another.
Index
A basket of assets tracked as one number, like the S&P 500.
Leverage
Controlling a large position with a smaller deposit. Magnifies gains and losses.
Limit order
An order to buy or sell at a set price or better.
Liquidity
How easily an asset can be traded without moving its price.
Long
A position that profits when price rises.
Lot
A standard trade size. In forex, 100,000 units of the base currency.
MACD
Moving Average Convergence Divergence, a momentum indicator based on two EMAs.
Margin
The deposit required to open a leveraged position.
Margin call
A demand to add funds when losses eat into the required margin.
Market order
An order to trade immediately at the best available price.
NFP
Non-farm payrolls, the monthly US jobs report.
Overbought
When price has risen fast and far, often RSI above 70.
Oversold
When price has fallen fast and far, often RSI below 30.
PCE
Personal Consumption Expenditures, the Fed's preferred inflation measure.
Pip
The smallest standard price step in forex, usually 0.0001.
Pivot point
A level calculated from the previous period's high, low and close, with support and resistance levels around it.
Position size
How many units or lots you trade, set by your risk and stop distance.
Pullback
A temporary move against the main trend.
Resistance
A price area where selling has repeatedly stopped a rise.
Risk to reward
The ratio of what a trade can lose to what it aims to gain.
RSI
Relative Strength Index, a 0–100 momentum oscillator.
Safe haven
An asset investors buy in times of stress, such as gold, the yen or US Treasuries.
Scalping
Very short-term trading aiming for small, frequent gains.
Short
A position that profits when price falls.
Slippage
The difference between the expected and actual fill price.
Spread
The gap between the bid and the ask.
Stop-loss
An order that closes a trade at a set price to cap the loss.
Support
A price area where buying has repeatedly stopped a fall.
Swing trading
Holding trades for days to weeks to capture a larger move.
Take-profit
An order that closes a trade at a set price to lock in a gain.
Trend
The general direction of price: higher highs and lows, or lower highs and lows.
Volatility
How much and how fast price moves.
VIX
An index of expected US stock market volatility, known as the fear gauge.
Yield
The return on a bond, expressed as an annual percentage.
